rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says kataba 'ala nafsihi occurs only here and in 6:54, always with reference to mercy; no other divine attribute is described this way.
rows.anchor: kataba 'ala nafsihi) occurs in the Qur'an only twice - here and in verse 54 of this surah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's mercy is further emphasized by 7:156, where His grace is said to overspread everything.
rows.anchor: This exceptional quality of God's grace and mercy is further stressed in 7:156 - "My grace overspreads everything"

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Asad calls it an authentic report that God's grace and mercy outstrip His wrath, transmitted by Bukhari and Muslim.
rows.anchor: authentic Tradition in which, according to the Prophet, God says of Himself, "Verily, My grace and mercy outstrips My wrath" (Bukhari and Muslim)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening the gates of good things after misery tests people through happiness.
rows.anchor: to test them by happiness after the test by misery.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ablasa means to despair of all hope or become broken in spirit; Asad links its linguistic root with Iblis's name.
rows.anchor: verb ablasa signifies "he despaired of all hope" or "became broken in spirit"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means that the last remnant was cut off.
rows.anchor: Lit., "cut off". The above passage illustrates a phenomenon

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the passage as illustrating the inevitable social and moral disintegration of communities that lose sight of spiritual truths.
rows.anchor: phenomenon well known in history: namely, the inevitable social and moral disintegration of communities which have lost sight of spiritual truths.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the image as satans enticing someone through earthly desires into bewilderment while companions call him back to guidance.
rows.anchor: whom the satans have enticed with lusts on earth, [rendering him] bewildered, [while] he has companions who call him unto guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to his note 11 on surah 10 for further explanation.
rows.anchor: See surah 10, note 11.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses remind readers not to turn food laws into ritual ends; Asad says their placement amid discussion of divine unity and faith underscores this purpose, and the errant views prioritize artificial ritual over spiritual values.
rows.anchor: the observance of such laws should not be made an end in itself and an object of ritual

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The errant views at issue stress artificial rituals and taboos instead of spiritual values.
rows.anchor: The "errant views" spoken of in verse 119 are such as lay stress on artificial rituals and taboos rather than on spiritual values.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders awliya'ihim literally as those who are near to the evil impulses and interprets shayatin as evil impulses, with cross-references to earlier notes.
rows.anchor: the satans whisper unto those who are near to them (ila awliya'ihim)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says people’s evil impulses argue to obscure God's clear food rules; obeying their arbitrary reasoning treats them as moral lawgivers and gives them a right belonging only to God.
rows.anchor: if you follow their arbitrary, deceptive reasoning, you will elevate them, as it were, to the position of moral law-givers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aghwahu can mean causing or allowing error, disappointing someone, or frustrating a desire; because Iblis lost his former angelic position, Asad prefers the sense that God thwarted him.
rows.anchor: Iblis refers to the loss of his erstwhile position among the angels, the rendering adopted by me seems to be the most appropriate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to 6:70 and its corresponding note for this description.
rows.anchor: See 6:70 and the corresponding note 60.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable's key point is that the power that makes plants grow will resurrect the dead at the end of time.
rows.anchor: by the exercise of the same life-giving power by which God causes plants to grow, He will resurrect the dead at the end of time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next line compares hearts open to truth with fertile land and deniers with barren land.
rows.anchor: those whose hearts are open to the voice of truth to fertile earth, and those who are bent on denying it, to barren earth.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari explains the idiom as having outrun something, that is, forsaken it or left it undone.
rows.anchor: The expression "one has outrun a forsaken it" or "left it undone" (Zamakhshari).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the Biblical account, Asad says the Qur'an does not accuse Aaron of making or worshipping the calf.
rows.anchor: the Qur'an does not accuse Aaron of having actually participated in making or worshipping the golden calf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says Aaron's guilt was passivity before idolatry, motivated by fear of splitting the people.
rows.anchor: his guilt consisted in having remained passive in the face of his people's idolatry for fear of causing a split among them

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi understands Moses' request as seeking forgiveness for his anger and harshness.
rows.anchor: Sc., "for my anger and my harshness" (Razi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across the Qur'an, the expression covers attributing divine qualities to objects or persons and fabricating statements about God, His attributes, or revelation.
rows.anchor: the attribution of divine qualities to any concrete or imaginary object or person, and (b) the making of false statements about God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here it means false imagery that diverts people from worshipping the One God.
rows.anchor: In the above context it refers to any false imagery which deflects man from the worship of the One God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that the phrase is literally "after it."
rows.anchor: Lit., "after'it".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where Exodus says Moses broke the tablets in anger, the Qur'anic narrative depicts them as intact.
rows.anchor: the Qur'anic narrative, however, shows them as having remained intact.

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take rajfah here to mean an earthquake, as it does elsewhere in the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators take rajfah to mean here "earthquake", as it evidently does in other places in the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says rajfah can mean any violent commotion or trembling; with no reason to assume an earthquake here, he takes it as the elders' intense regret and fear of punishment.
rows.anchor: we may assume that the violent trembling which seized the seventy elders was caused by their intense regret and fear of God's punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the promise that God's grace overspreads everything to 6:12 and 6:54 and the corresponding note 10.
rows.anchor: Cf. 6:12 (and the corresponding note 10), as well as 6:54.
